fieldMarks: Usually black, especially in eastern North America; western animals are often brown, cinnamon or blonde, and some coastal British Columbia and Alaska bears are creamy white or bluish-grey.
Pale muzzle contrasting with darker fur; sometimes a white chest spot.
Compared with grizzly/brown bears: longer, less heavily furred ears, a smaller shoulder hump and a convex rather than concave (dished) facial profile.
Males larger: males 47-409 kg, females 39-236 kg.
behavior: Generally active at dawn and dusk; near human food it may become daytime-active (roadsides) or nocturnal (campgrounds).
Mostly solitary except females with cubs, summer breeding pairs and gatherings at concentrated food sources.
Diet is mostly plant: grasses and forbs in spring, soft fruit in summer, and hard and soft mast in fall; animal food is mainly colonial insects and carrion.
Spends winter in dens; cubs are born in January-February while the female is dormant.
habitat: Prime habitat is relatively inaccessible terrain with thick understorey and abundant fruit or nut crops: hardwood-conifer forest in the Northeast, oak-hickory and swampy lowlands in the Southeast, and chaparral and pinyon-juniper at 900-3,000 m in the Southwest.
range: From northern Alaska east across virtually all of Canada to Labrador and Newfoundland, and south through much of the United States into central Mexico.

lookalikes.name: Grizzly (brown) bear
lookalikes.howToTell: The grizzly has a larger shoulder hump, shorter, furrier ears and a concave (dished) profile; colour alone is unreliable because black bears can be brown, cinnamon or blonde.
